Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our discovery call and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

- Primary goal: integrate streaming summarization for provider notes to reduce manual QA time while keeping regulatory traceability.
- Key constraints you mentioned: PII handling, 99th-percentile latency target <= 450ms for partial responses, and preserving stop-sequence behavior for multi-segment notes.
- Current data: ~200k tokens/day, 95% single-conversation sessions <= 800 tokens.

Next steps I propose:
1) Marissa and Rishi to share model-fit recommendations + a small prompt set we can run through a quick POC.
2) We’ll run a short streaming-quality benchmark (coherence, stop-sequence reliability, latency) and share results.
3) Quick sync next week to review POC findings and contract parameters.

I’ve looped in Marissa (product/solutions) and Rishi (engineer) to own the model suggestions and the streaming UX tests.

Best,

Hi Alex / Priya —

Great to meet you both. Per Jordan’s recap, I put together an initial recommendation and a small prompt set (attached) you can use for the POC. High-level recommendations: 

- Recommended models (fast/economical tier): redwood-compat-gpt-3o-quant (for short summaries, best latency/cost tradeoff).
- Recommended models (quality-first tier): redwood-rlhf-1.2 (longer context, stronger factuality and stop-sequence handling).
- For streaming specifically, we recommend starting with redwood-compat-gpt-3o-quant and tuning the stop sequences at the application layer (see notes below) to hit the latency target and then validate quality against the quality-tier model.

Attached: acme_benchmark_results_v2.pdf (initial heuristic benchmarks on a similar dataset) and prompt_set_acme_health.jsonl (5 prompt/expected-output pairs we used for the bench).

Streaming UX notes / quick mitigations:
- Partial output coherence: implement a lightweight post-token stabilization window (150–200ms) before emitting early partial segments for UI; this reduces mid-stream hallucination while keeping perceived latency low.
- Stop sequences: prefer application-level stop enforcement (detect EOT tokens + regex on trailing punctuation) because some quantized runtimes emit fragmented stops.
- Latency: target per-token processing budget <= 30ms on the dedicated inf nodes; we’ll include batching config in the POC.

Next steps: If you’re ok, we’ll run a 48-hour streaming benchmark on a preserved prompt subset and then share results + a short recording of the stream behavior. Jordan — do you want me to create a HubSpot activity and attach the benchmark doc?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole

Alex / Priya — quick technical answers and what we’ll measure in the POC: 

1) Stop-sequence behavior: the fragmented stop issue shows up more frequently on the quantized runtimes (redwood-compat-gpt-3o-quant) when the model emits punctuation-heavy stops across token boundaries. The quality-tier model (redwood-rlhf-1.2) is more consistent but costs ~3x tokens computation. For the POC we can run both in parallel and compare.

2) Stabilization window latency: in practice adding a 150–200ms buffer before emitting an early segment increases perceived end-to-end by ~150–200ms but reduces incoherent mid-stream chunks by ~30–40% (based on internal telemetry). We can tune that down for strict latency requirements.

3) PII: strongly recommend a two-layer approach: pre-stream deterministic masking (PII regex + field redaction) + in-flight token filtering for residuals. We’ll share a small masking script as part of the POC.

What we’ll measure in the 48-hour POC:
- Coherence score (human eval + automated n-gram overlap)
- Stop-sequence failure rate (per 1k streams)
- 95th/99th percentile partial-response latency
- Cost per 1k tokens (compare quantized vs quality-tier)

If that sounds good, please upload the 200 de-identified notes to the secure share link and we’ll provision a POC run (expected turnaround 48 hours once data arrives).

–Rishi
